graph_authoring_scope.aspect_name: Operating systems and CPU virtualization foundations
graph_authoring_scope.aspect_description: Diagnosable concepts from OSTEP Chapter 2 and Chapters 4-8: operating-system goals, process abstraction and API, limited direct execution, basic CPU scheduling metrics and policies, and multi-level feedback queues.
representative_tasks: Explain how an operating system turns physical resources into easier-to-use virtual abstractions.
Distinguish the operating system's roles as virtual machine, standard interface provider, and resource manager.
Explain why protection is necessary when multiple programs share CPU, memory, and devices.
Distinguish mechanism from policy using CPU virtualization as an example.
Explain why a running program is not the same thing as its executable file.
Identify the major components of a process's machine state.
Distinguish running, ready, and blocked process states in an execution trace.
Predict legal process-state transitions after dispatch, I/O initiation, I/O completion, and preemption.
Explain why a process list or process control block is needed by the operating system.
Use process identifiers and parent-child relationships to interpret a process tree.
Predict the possible outputs of a program that calls fork without assuming a fixed parent-child execution order.
Explain how fork creates a new process while preserving distinct return values in parent and child.
Explain how exec changes a process image without creating a new process identifier.
Explain how wait supports ordering and resource collection between parent and child processes.
Distinguish normal process termination from a zombie or orphan process situation.
Choose among fork, exec, wait, and exit for a stated process-management goal.
Explain how a shell uses fork, exec, and wait to launch a foreground command.
Explain why unrestricted direct execution would prevent the OS from retaining control.
Distinguish user mode from kernel mode and identify operations that require privileged execution.
Trace a system call through trap entry, kernel handling, and return to user mode.
Distinguish a system call trap from a hardware interrupt and from a program exception.
Explain why a timer interrupt is needed to regain control from a CPU-bound process.
Trace the steps of a context switch between two processes.
Identify which process state must be saved and restored across a context switch.
Explain the difference between cooperative and preemptive approaches to CPU sharing.
Diagnose why disabling interrupts is not a safe general solution for untrusted user programs.
Calculate turnaround time for a workload under a specified schedule.
Calculate response time and distinguish it from turnaround time.
Explain why a policy that minimizes turnaround time may provide poor interactive response.
Schedule a set of jobs under first-in-first-out and compute completion metrics.
Construct a convoy-effect example and explain why FIFO performs poorly on it.
Schedule known jobs under shortest-job-first and explain its optimality assumptions.
Explain why non-preemptive shortest-job-first struggles when job lengths are unknown or arrivals differ.
Schedule jobs under shortest-time-to-completion-first with staggered arrivals.
Explain how preemption changes shortest-job-first into shortest-time-to-completion-first.
Simulate round-robin scheduling for a given time slice and arrival sequence.
Predict how a smaller round-robin quantum affects response time and context-switch overhead.
Compare FIFO, SJF, STCF, and round robin for batch and interactive workloads.
Explain why an online scheduler cannot generally know a job's future CPU demand.
State the goals of a multi-level feedback queue when job behavior is not known in advance.
Apply MLFQ priority rules to select the next runnable job.
Trace how a CPU-bound job's priority changes as it consumes its time allotment.
Explain why an interactive or I/O-bound job may remain at high priority in MLFQ.
Diagnose starvation in an MLFQ workload containing a stream of interactive jobs.
Explain how periodic priority boosting addresses starvation.
Construct a gaming attack against a naive MLFQ rule and explain why it works.
Explain how cumulative allotment accounting reduces MLFQ gaming opportunities.
Predict the effect of changing queue allotments and time quanta on scheduler behavior.
Compare scheduler fairness with optimization of turnaround and response time.
Integrate process abstraction, protected execution, context switching, and scheduling into one CPU-virtualization trace.
excluded_topics: Virtual-memory address spaces, paging, segmentation, TLBs, and swapping
Threads, synchronization, locks, condition variables, semaphores, and concurrency bugs
I/O devices, disks, RAID, filesystems, persistence, and distributed systems
Lottery scheduling and multiprocessor scheduling beyond brief contrast
Linux CFS and production-kernel implementation details not developed in Chapters 2 and 4-8
Architecture-specific register layouts and assembly details
Programming-project setup and simulator command-line memorization
Historical anecdotes that do not support a reusable operating-system concept
Performance claims that ignore the workload assumptions stated in the selected chapters
